title: World War 1 Quiz: 20 Questions on the Great War
description: Test your knowledge of World War I with 20 free questions on key battles, treaties, and events. Easy to expert, with an explanation after each answer.
h1: World War 1 Quiz: How Well Do You Know the Great War?
intro: The First World War reshaped the map of the world and the lives of millions. This World War 1 quiz tests your knowledge of the causes, the battles, the weapons, and the peace settlement of 1919. The first eight questions cover the essentials most people know, the middle eight ask about specific battles, leaders, and treaties, and the last four are expert-level. You have about five seconds per question, and every answer comes with a short explanation that gives context in a neutral, factual way. It's free, quick, and a good way to remember a pivotal period. Let's begin!

questions.q: Which event on June 28, 1914, set off the crisis that led to World War I?
choices: The death of Kaiser Wilhelm II
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
questions.explication: The heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne was shot in Sarajevo, and within weeks the great powers were at war.

questions.q: On what date did the armistice stop the fighting on the Western Front?
questions.explication: The armistice was signed in a railway carriage near Compiègne and took effect at 11 a.m., the "eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month."

questions.q: What type of fighting dominated the Western Front from late 1914?
questions.explication: Machine guns and artillery made advancing so deadly that both sides dug trenches stretching from the North Sea to Switzerland.

questions.q: Which 1916 battle lasted about ten months and became a symbol of the war's attrition?
questions.explication: The Battle of Verdun produced roughly 700,000 casualties on both sides for very little change in the front line.

questions.q: Which country joined the Allies in April 1917?
questions.explication: The U.S. declared war on Germany on April 6, 1917, after unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram.

questions.q: Which neutral country did Germany invade in August 1914 to bypass French defenses?
questions.explication: A key reason Britain entered the war was Germany's violation of Belgian neutrality, which Britain had pledged to protect.

questions.q: Germany and Austria-Hungary were part of which alliance?
questions.explication: The Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria later joined the Central Powers, while Britain, France, and Russia formed the Entente.

questions.q: In which year did World War I begin?
questions.explication: The fighting lasted more than four years and involved more than 30 countries.

questions.q: Which September 1914 battle halted the German advance toward Paris?
choices: The First Battle of the Marne
questions.explication: French and British forces counterattacked along the river Marne, forcing the Germans to retreat and ending hopes of a quick victory.

questions.q: Which treaty signed in June 1919 imposed terms on Germany?
questions.explication: It required Germany to accept responsibility for the war, pay reparations, and give up territory.

questions.q: Which Allied commander accepted the German armistice in 1918?
questions.explication: Marshal Foch served as Supreme Allied Commander in 1918 and received the German delegation in his railway carriage.

questions.q: Which gas did the German army use on a large scale at Ypres in April 1915?
questions.explication: The attack at Ypres was among the first large-scale uses of poison gas, and it led to the development of gas masks.

questions.q: Which new weapon appeared on the battlefield at the Somme in September 1916?
questions.explication: British tanks first rolled into battle on September 15, 1916, but they were slow and unreliable at first.

questions.q: Which March 1918 treaty ended the war between Russia and the Central Powers?
questions.explication: The Bolshevik government gave up large territories to leave the war, though the treaty was annulled after Germany's defeat.

questions.q: Which 1916 North Sea clash was the largest naval battle of the war?
questions.explication: The British and German fleets both claimed success, but Germany's fleet stayed in port for most of the rest of the war.

questions.q: Which empire, centered on Constantinople, joined the Central Powers in late 1914?
questions.explication: The Ottomans fought in the Middle East, the Caucasus, and at Gallipoli, and the empire collapsed after the war.

questions.q: Which British ocean liner was sunk by a German submarine in May 1915?
questions.explication: The sinking killed nearly 1,200 people, including 128 Americans, and strengthened anti-German sentiment abroad.

questions.q: Which January 1917 telegram proposed a German alliance with Mexico?
questions.explication: British intelligence intercepted and decoded the message, and its publication helped push the United States toward war.

questions.q: Which 1917 battle in Belgium became a byword for mud and heavy casualties?
questions.explication: The Third Battle of Ypres, fought from July to November 1917, gained little ground at a high cost.

questions.q: Which strait was the target of the failed Allied campaign of 1915?
questions.explication: The Gallipoli campaign tried to open a sea route to Russia and knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war, but it ended in evacuation.

faq: Historians point to a mix of long-term tensions, including alliances, militarism, imperial rivalries, and nationalism. The immediate trigger was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914. A chain of ultimatums and mobilizations then pulled the major powers into war.
How long did World War I last?

It lasted from July 1914 to November 1918, a little over four years. Fighting on the Western Front stopped with the armistice of November 11, 1918, but the formal peace settlement came with the Treaty of Versailles, signed on June 28, 1919, five years to the day after the assassination in Sarajevo.
Which countries fought in World War I?

The two main sides were the Allies, including Britain, France, Russia, Italy, Japan, and later the United States, and the Central Powers: Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria. Troops also came from colonies and dominions across Africa, Asia, and the Americas.
